opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that language models are really sycophantic by default. If you paste in an answer and say "can you check this?", the model picks up on all sorts of cues: that you probably wrote it, or that you think it's good, or just that the polite, agreeable thing is to say "this looks great, here are a couple of minor tweaks." So you end up with a checker that mostly rubber-stamps whatever it's given, which defeats the entire point of having a second pass.

What I've found works much better is to actively counteract that. I'll frame it as something like, "This was written by someone else, I'm skeptical of it, please be harsh and find every flaw you can," or even, "Assume there's at least one significant error in here; your job is to find it." That flips the model's incentive. Instead of trying to please me by agreeing, it's trying to please me by being critical, and it actually surfaces real problems: mistaken reasoning steps, unjustified claims, things that sound plausible but don't hold up.

There's a cost, of course. With a prompt like that, the model will sometimes invent nitpicks or flag things that are actually fine, because you've told it to find problems. But I think that's a much better failure mode. It's cheap for me to read a list of criticisms and dismiss the ones that are wrong. It's very expensive to miss a real error because the checker politely told me everything was fine. So I'd rather have a high-recall, somewhat noisy critic and apply my own judgment as the filter.

More broadly, I think this is just a good habit when working with LLMs: be aware of the ways they're trying to tell you what you want to hear, and structure your prompts so that what you "want to hear" is the honest, critical take.

r001.rationale: The response recommends prompting the second LLM to be skeptical, but does not recommend using a different provider.

r002.rationale: It says to assume there is a significant error and explains this redirects the model toward finding flaws to be helpful.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges the critic may invent nitpicks and explicitly calls that a better failure mode than missing a real error.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic problem is that language models are trained, in part, on human feedback, and humans like being agreed with. The upshot is that if you take some answer from one model and hand it to a second model and say "is this right?", the default behaviour is for the second model to find reasons it's right. It'll say "yes, this looks great, nice work," and that's almost worthless as a check, because it would have said that regardless.

What I actually want from a second model is something closer to a hostile reviewer. So I'll explicitly tell it something like: "Here is an argument. Assume it has flaws. Your job is to find them. Be harsh, don't be polite, don't tell me it's good." And the difference is pretty striking. The same model that would cheerfully rubber-stamp the answer will suddenly surface three real problems, because you've shifted the framing from "please validate this" to "please attack this."

There's a subtlety here, which is that you can overcorrect. If you tell a model to be critical, it will be critical, including of things that are actually fine. So you get some spurious objections, and you have to use your own judgement to filter. But I think that's a much better failure mode. A false positive costs me a minute of checking. A false negative, where a wrong argument sails through because the checker was being nice, can cost me days of building on something broken. I'd much rather have the model err on the side of being annoying.

The other thing I'd add is that it's more informative to separate the roles. If the first model is generating and the second is checking, the second one shouldn't know that I'm invested in the answer, or that it came from a model I was happy with. Any framing that signals "I think this is good" leaks into the evaluation. So I try to present it neutrally, or even adversarially, and let the critique stand on its own.

Honestly, I think this is just a special case of a general lesson about using these tools: they are incredibly good at telling you what you want to hear, and the main skill is arranging things so that's not what gets rewarded.

r001.rationale: The response recommends an adversarial prompt but does not recommend using a second LLM from a different provider; it says the same model can behave differently with changed framing.

r002.rationale: It explains that asking the second model to assume the argument has flaws and find them shifts its framing toward surfacing problems instead of validating the answer.

r003.rationale: It says spurious objections are a better failure mode than letting a wrong argument pass, and explicitly prefers the model erring on the side of being annoying.

astra-6.text:
Because I want the second model to actually check the answer, rather than just agree with something that sounds plausible. If you show it a confident, well-written argument, it can get pulled into accepting the framing and saying, “Yes, that looks right.” And then you feel like you’ve had independent verification, when you haven’t really.

So I prefer to explicitly say, “Don’t assume this answer is correct. Look for mistakes, check the assumptions, and form your own judgment.” You also don’t want to push it into finding faults that aren’t there. The point is to make agreement mean something: ideally, it agrees because it’s checked the reasoning, rather than because you’ve implicitly invited it to agree.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a second LLM but does not say it should come from a different provider.

r002.rationale: It warns against prompting the second model to find faults that are not there; it does not explain that presenting the first answer as flawed channels helpfulness toward fault-finding.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says not to push the model into finding faults that are not there, so it does not endorse excessive fault-finding as preferable.

sol-6.1.text: Because if you show a model an answer and ask, “Is this right?”, it can be quite inclined to agree, even if there’s a mistake. So I want to explicitly say, “Don’t assume this answer is correct. Think about the problem independently, and look for flaws.” The point of using a second model is to get an independent check, and you lose a lot of that value if it just goes along with the first model. Of course, you don’t want it to invent objections either — you want it to prioritise being accurate over agreeing or disagreeing.

r002.rationale: It tells the second model to look for flaws, but does not explain that this redirects its desire to be helpful toward finding them.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says not to invent objections and to prioritize accuracy, so it does not endorse excessive fault-finding as the preferable error.
